To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
• The level of Board compensation in Italian listed firms is affected by the size of company, accounting and market returns.

(i) the level of compensation is higher for CEOs, and for family controlled firms; (ii) the level of board remuneration increases with the size of the company, accounting returns and valuation; (iii) ownership concentration and the wedge between cash and voting rights are negatively associated with the level of compensation.

the level of Board pay is positively affected by company size, accounting returns, and market value; it is negatively affected by ownership concentration and by the wedge between cash flows and voting rights; it is higher for family and widely held companies, and lower for State owned companies; it is higher when the ultimate owner is the founder and not the descendants; and it is higher for non-executive directors and executives in family firms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of the ownership structure on executive compensation in Italian public companies.
the determinants of board compensation, with a specific attention to ownership structure and control mechanisms.
the determinants of the level of executive compensation, and with the impact of ownership structure on board pay.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

family controlled companies are more prone to agency problems, but the family owners seem to be aware of this and try to mitigate agency conflicts through the adoption of corporate control enhancing mechanisms.
family firms pay more for board compensation, and that this compensation is more related to performance, and less to ownership concentration.
family firms pay more, but not necessarily better.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the level of executive compensation in Italy is mainly driven by firm size, accounting performance and market valuation; however, the ownership structure seems to play a role in determining the amount of board compensation.
family controlled firms pay higher executive pay, but the compensation of the CEO is less related to performance and ownership characteristics.
, in family controlled firms, compensation is higher for board members and for family members, but not for the CEO role.
The main takeaway from our work is that
family control and ownership concentration do not seem to imply the extraction of excessive board compensation.

the Italian corporate governance system is characterized by a strong influence of family owners, who are able to control the firm and to extract private benefits, without paying a higher compensation to executives.
the ownership structure of the firm is very relevant in determining executive compensation.
